extracted.intended_audience: employers, labor lawyers, policymakers, worker advocates, and other stakeholders participating in or subject to the FTC non-compete rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory preamble describing legal standards, definitions, and interpretive guidance used by the FTC to determine its jurisdiction and to define and scope prohibited non-compete clauses and related restrictive employment terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 5 legal standard for unfair methods of competition
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 5 of the FTC Act, the Commission assesses two elements: (1) whether the conduct is a method of competition, as opposed to a condition of the marketplace, and (2) whether it is unfair, meaning that it goes beyond competition on the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The latter (unfairness) inquiry has two components: (a) whether the conduct has indicia of unfairness and (b) whether the conduct tends to negatively affect competitive conditions, weighed on a sliding scale. Section 5 does not limit indicia to conduct that benefits one firm and disadvantages others; restrictive or exclusionary conduct may be unlawful even if it benefits specific firms while tending to negatively affect competitive conditions. Section 5 does not require a separate showing of market power or market definition and does not import the Sherman Act rule-of-reason analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicia of unfairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicia of unfairness include the extent to which the conduct may be coercive, exploitative, collusive, abusive, deceptive, predatory, or involve the use of economic power of a similar nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicia may also be present if the conduct is otherwise restrictive or exclusionary depending on circumstances (nature of commercial setting, current and potential future effects). Where indicia of unfairness are clear (e.g., coercive and exploitative conduct), only a limited showing of tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions may be required. Examples: coercion of dealers to buy particular products (Atlantic Refining; Texaco), exploiting inability of children to protect themselves (Keppel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: The inquiry focuses on the nature and tendency of the conduct; it does not turn on whether the conduct directly caused actual harm in the specific instance and does not require a detailed economic analysis or current anticompetitive effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inquiry examines whether the conduct has a tendency to raise prices, reduce output, limit choice, lower quality, reduce innovation, impair or exclude other market participants, reduce the likelihood of potential or nascent competition, reduce labor mobility, suppress worker compensation, or degrade working conditions. These concerns may be assessed in the aggregate (e.g., similar conduct by multiple firms). Courts have found unlawful tendencies without full-scale economic proofs (e.g., Union Circulation Company; Brown Shoe; Motion Picture Advertising Service Co.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sliding-scale evidentiary approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission weighs indicia of unfairness and tendency to negatively affect competitive conditions on a sliding scale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If indicia of unfairness are strong (clear coercion/exploitation), only a limited showing of tendency is needed. If indicia are less clear, a stronger showing of tendency is required. Past Commission and court decisions have found violations based primarily on clear indicia without detailed economic analysis; in other instances, tendency evidence has sufficed without focusing on indicia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of asserted justifications
rubrics_metrics.description: When defendants assert justifications as affirmative defenses, courts and the Commission evaluate them and have often declined to consider some justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pecuniary benefit to the party responsible for the conduct is not cognizable as a justification. Where justifications are considered, they must be legally cognizable, non-pretextual, and any restriction used to bring about the benefit must be narrowly tailored to limit adverse impact on competitive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commission jurisdiction over entities claiming nonprofit/tax-exempt status
rubrics_metrics.description: Tax-exempt status is a factor but not dispositive for whether an entity is a corporation organized for profit under the FTC Act; IRS findings that an entity does not qualify for tax-exempt status are meaningful to the Commission's analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative and judicial decisions have found private benefits (e.g., organizations operating on behalf of for-profit physician members; associations contracting with payers on behalf of for-profit members) can render an entity organized for pecuniary benefit and within FTC jurisdiction. IRS precedent finds loss of tax-exempt status where a purported nonprofit 'has ceded effective control' to a for-profit partner or pays unreasonable/percentage-based compensation to insiders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'business entity' for the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission adopts 'business entity' as 'a partnership, corporation, association, limited liability company, or other legal entity, or a division or subsidiary thereof.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition was retained (no functional test adopted) to apply the sale-of-a-business exception where a person is selling a division or subsidiary. The Commission declined to add a 25% ownership threshold and concluded 'other legal entity' already captures general partnerships and trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale-of-business exception approach
rubrics_metrics.description: The sale-of-a-business exception was discussed in relation to the definition of 'business entity' and proposed ownership thresholds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission eliminated the 25% ownership threshold in the final rule's sale-of-a-business exception to avoid incentives for employers to restructure to evade the exception and to provide clarity to workers and employers. The Commission declined a functional test for 'business entity' to avoid complexity and uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'employment'
rubrics_metrics.description: The final rule defines 'employment' as 'work for a person' to ensure coverage of workers regardless of their legal classification under other laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation is intended to cover workers hired through staffing agencies, professional employer organizations, loan-out arrangements, affiliates, persons who share control over the worker's work, externs, interns, and volunteers—i.e., employment exists for purposes of the rule regardless of whether an employment relationship exists under other Federal or State labor law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision not to adopt a standalone definition of 'employer'
rubrics_metrics.description: After considering comments, the Commission did not finalize a separate definition of 'employer.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instead, the Commission revised the definitions of 'non-compete clause' and 'worker' (and used 'work for a person' for employment) so that coverage extends to workers even where the person who hired or contracted with them differs from the person for whom they work; the approach avoids enumerating many complex employment arrangements and aims to capture indirect employment relationships generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope of 'non-compete clause'
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 910.1 defines 'non-compete clause' as a term or condition of employment that prohibits a worker from, penalizes a worker for, or functions to prevent a worker from (A) seeking or accepting work in the United States with a different person where such work would begin after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition; or (B) operating a business in the United States after the conclusion of the employment that includes the term or condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For these purposes, 'term or condition of employment' 'includes, but is not limited to, a contractual term or workplace policy, whether written or oral.' The definition applies to express prohibitions, penalties (e.g., liquidated damages), and de facto or functional non-competes (agreements that effectively prevent post-employment work or business). Examples: explicit multi-year, geographic prohibitions; liquidated damages clauses ($50,000 example); withholding/forfeiture of promised compensation or benefits as a penalty for post-employment work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage and treatment of functional non-competes and related restrictive covenants
rubrics_metrics.description: The rule covers 'functional' or 'de facto' non-competes—restrictive employment agreements that, although not labeled a non-compete, have the effect of preventing post-employment work or business—and addresses related covenants (NDAs, TRAPs, non-solicitation, no-hire, no-business/non-dealing, forfeiture-for-competition, garden leave).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative functional non-competes include overbroad NDAs that effectively preclude work in the same field and TRAPs requiring payment not reasonably related to training costs. Commenters raised divergent views: some urged broader coverage or bans (e.g., on abusive TRAPs), others warned of overbreadth/vagueness and harm to legitimate NDAs or deferred compensation arrangements. The Commission slightly modified the definition to clarify scope and included examples/considerations (e.g., that TRAP penalties reasonably related to employer's training costs may not be functional non-competes, while abusive TRAPs can be). For non-solicitation/no-hire/garden leave/forfeiture clauses, the Commission considered comments about when such clauses are functionally equivalent to non-competes and whether to exclude or clarify treatment; commenters asked for durational limits, express carve-outs, or explicit coverage depending on coercion/effect.
